1.text:
How Does a Star's Mass Decide Its Death?

In Deck 16 we watched stars being born. Now we finish their life story. Some stars fade quietly for trillions of years. Some puff off glowing shells of gas. And some explode so brightly they outshine whole galaxies.

What decides which path a star takes? One thing: its mass. This deck asks, how does a star's mass decide the way it dies? Along the way you'll meet red giants, white dwarfs, pulsars, black holes, and even the stars that made the gold in a ring and the carbon in your body.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist. Copy these as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can compare how long stars of different masses live. I can sort low, medium and high mass stars by how they end. I can describe red giants, planetary nebulae and white dwarfs. I can model the life span of the Sun, from birth to white dwarf. I can explain why fusion stops at iron and the core collapses.

I can use SN 1987A's neutrinos as evidence for core collapse. I can describe neutron stars, pulsars and black holes. I can trace stars of different masses on the H-R diagram. I can explain where elements heavier than iron come from. And I can explain Type Ia supernovae and neutron-star mergers. These connect to Indiana standards ES.1.4, ES.2.3 and ES.1.2, plus some enrichment.

3.text:
Big Stars Die Young

You might think bigger stars live longer, since they have more fuel. It's the opposite. A star's lifetime goes as mass ÷ luminosity, and big stars burn fuel fastest. It's like a huge truck with a giant gas tank that burns through gas so fast it runs dry before a small car does.

Look at the numbers. An O5 star of 40 Suns lives about 1 million years. A B0 star of 16 Suns lives 10 million years. An A0 star of 3.3 Suns lives 500 million years. The Sun lives about 10 billion years. And an M0 star of about 0.5 Suns lives roughly 80 billion years.

Put another way, the Sun's life is 10,000 times longer than a 40-Sun O5 star's. Compare that to the universe so far: 13.8 billion years. Some small stars will outlive the current age of the universe many times over.

4.text:
Three Ways to End

Stars follow one of three paths, depending on their mass. Low-mass stars, below about 0.2 Suns, are red dwarfs. They grow slowly hotter for trillions of years and end as helium white dwarfs. But none has died yet, because the universe isn't old enough!

Medium-mass stars, about 0.2 to 8 Suns, like the Sun, follow this path: main sequence, then red giant, then planetary nebula, then white dwarf.

A high-mass star is a star born with more than about 8 Suns, and it ends in a supernova. Its path goes from a blue main sequence star to a red supergiant, then a supernova, leaving behind a neutron star or a black hole.

Did you know? Red dwarfs never become red giants because convection keeps stirring their whole inside, so they burn almost all their hydrogen.

Check for Understanding: Part 1

Time to sort some stars. Which of these stars will NEVER become a red giant?

Is it A) a 0.1-Sun red dwarf, B) the Sun, C) a 3-Sun star, or D) a 20-Sun star? Use the three paths on Slide 4 to decide.

6.text:
When the Hydrogen Runs Out

Eventually, a star's core runs out of hydrogen. A red giant is an aging star whose core is out of hydrogen, so its outer layers swell and cool.

Here's what happens inside. The helium core has no fusion, so gravity squeezes it, and it shrinks and heats up. That heat starts hydrogen still fusing in a shell around the core. The extra energy pushes the outer layers out until they're huge and cooler, so they glow red.

A Sun-like star swells to about 100 times wider than it is now. On the slide, the Sun today is drawn to scale as the tiny dot next to the giant.

Did you know? If the Sun were a red giant 100 times wider, it would stretch about halfway to Earth's orbit.

7.text:
The Helium Flash

The helium core keeps shrinking and heating until it hits 100 million K, the core temperature where helium starts to fuse. That's almost seven times hotter than the Sun's core today.

Helium fuses through the triple-alpha process: 3 helium (⁴He) make 1 carbon (¹²C). Then carbon plus one more helium makes oxygen. In stars of about 0.8 to 2 Suns, the whole core ignites in a flash, a sudden runaway burst.

After the flash, the star settles into a steady stretch of helium fusion that astronomers call the horizontal branch, because of where these stars line up on the H-R diagram.

Did you know? It's called "triple-alpha" because a helium nucleus is also known as an alpha particle.

8.text:
A Gentle Goodbye

At the last stage, a Sun-like star becomes an AGB star with two fusion shells, one fusing helium and one fusing hydrogen. Its outer layers are loosely held, and they drift away.

A planetary nebula is the glowing shell of gas a dying giant puffs off into space. The gas drifts out at 20 to 30 km/s, and a typical one is about 1 light-year across. The Ring Nebula, shown here in a Webb image, is a famous example. The hot core left behind becomes a new white dwarf, and its ultraviolet light makes the shell glow.

The name is misleading: planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets. It's an old name from when small telescopes made them look like fuzzy round planets.

9.text:
The White Dwarf Limit

When fusion ends, what's left is a white dwarf. It's held up by squeezed electrons, not by fusion. Electrons can only be packed so tightly, and they push back hard.

A white dwarf is about the same size as Earth, but with the mass of a whole star. And oddly, heavier white dwarfs are smaller. Look at the graph: as mass climbs from 0.5 to 1.0 to 1.4 Suns, the radius shrinks.

There's a limit. The Chandrasekhar limit, 1.4 Suns, is the most mass a white dwarf can hold. Sirius B, at 25,400 K and 1.02 Suns, is safely below it.

Did you know? A teaspoon of white dwarf material would weigh several tons on Earth.

10.text:
The Sun's Future

Let's map the Sun's whole life on a timeline, in billions of years after the Sun formed. Earth forms 4.54 billion years ago. Today we're past the 4 billion mark. The Sun brightens slowly the whole time, as you learned in Deck 14.

In about 1 billion years from now, the Sun will be bright enough that Earth's oceans boil away. In about 5 billion years, the Sun swells into a red giant about 100 times wider.

At the end, the Sun leaves a white dwarf with about half the Sun's mass. The rest of its mass drifts off into space.

Did you know? As a red giant, the Sun will swallow Mercury and Venus, and probably Earth too.

12.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Think about the Sun's future. What will the Sun leave behind when it dies?

Is it A) a white dwarf inside a planetary nebula, B) a neutron star, C) a black hole, or D) nothing, because it explodes completely? Look back at Slides 4, 8 and 9 and choose.

13.text:
Betelgeuse, a Red Supergiant

A red supergiant is a massive star near the end of its life, swollen to enormous size. The most famous one is Betelgeuse, the red shoulder of Orion.

How big is it? Look at the slide. If you put Betelgeuse where the Sun is, it would reach past Earth's orbit and Mars's orbit, though not quite out to Jupiter's. It gives off about 90,000 times the Sun's power and sits about 550 light-years away.

From 2019 to 2020, Betelgeuse faded in what's called the Great Dimming. People wondered if it was about to explode, but it turned out to be a cloud of dust that the star had puffed out. Betelgeuse is a future supernova, but it's too far to hurt us.

Did you know? When Betelgeuse does explode, it may be bright enough to see in the daytime.

14.text:
Layers Like an Onion

Massive stars don't stop at helium. They keep going with shell burning: fusion in layers around the core, each one making heavier elements. From the outside in, the layers are hydrogen, helium, carbon, neon, oxygen, silicon, and iron at the center. (The drawing is not to scale.)

Each new fuel burns faster than the last. Carbon lasts about 2,000 years. Silicon lasts only days. The star is running out of time, and the clock keeps speeding up.

Then it hits a wall. In the iron core, fusing iron uses up energy instead of making it. Iron is the dead end. With no energy coming out of the core, nothing holds the star up against gravity.

15.text:
The Iron Core Collapses

What happens next is fast. In under 1 second, an Earth-size iron core crushes down to under 20 km across. That's like squeezing a planet down to the size of a city.

The pressure is so great that electrons squeeze into protons, making neutrons plus neutrinos. The core becomes a neutron core about 20 km wide, and neutrinos pour out. The neutrinos blast the outer layers away, and the star blows apart.

This is a Type II supernova. It throws at least 5 Suns of gas out into space.

Did you know? For a few weeks, one supernova can shine as bright as billions of Suns.

16.text:
SN 1987A: A Message in Neutrinos

On February 23, 1987, a supernova went off in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near ours, about 160,000 light-years away. It was named SN 1987A.

The remarkable part is that about two dozen neutrinos from that one supernova were caught on Earth. Kamiokande II caught 11 or 12, IMB caught 8, and Baksan caught 5. These detectors are giant water tanks deep underground. The neutrinos pass straight through Earth, and they arrived before anyone saw the light.

Why does that matter? Neutrinos are made in core collapse, when electrons squeeze into protons. Catching them was direct evidence that the core really did collapse, just as the model predicted.

Did you know? SN 1987A was bright enough to see with the unaided eye from the Southern Hemisphere.

17.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

Let's test the big idea of Part 3. Why does fusion in a massive star stop at iron?

Is it A) fusing iron uses up energy instead of releasing it, B) iron is too heavy for gravity to squeeze, C) the star runs out of hydrogen first, or D) iron is too cold to fuse? Look back at Slides 14 and 15 and make your choice.

18.text:
Neutron Stars and Pulsars

A neutron star packs 1.4 to 2 Suns into a ball only 10 to 20 km across. That's more than the Sun's mass squeezed into a city-sized ball.

Some neutron stars are pulsars. A pulsar is a spinning neutron star whose beams sweep past Earth like a lighthouse. Look at the slide: there's a spin axis, and a beam comes from each magnetic pole. Each sweep past Earth is one blip.

The first pulsar was found by Jocelyn Bell Burnell with Antony Hewish in 1967, with a pulse every 1.33728 s. The Crab pulsar, left by the supernova of 1054, spins so fast it sends 30 pulses a second.

Did you know? A teaspoon of neutron star material would weigh about as much as a mountain.

19.text:
Black Holes

If a dead core over about 3 Suns collapses, nothing can stop it. It collapses forever and becomes a black hole. Its edge is called the event horizon: inside it, not even light can escape.

Black holes are surprisingly small. A 1-Sun black hole would have a horizon only about 3 km in radius.

If light can't escape, how do we find them? We watch them eat. In Cygnus X-1 (shown as a drawing), a black hole of about 21 Suns is pulling gas off its partner star. That gas forms a hot disk that glows in X-rays before it falls in.

Did you know? To become a black hole, Earth would have to be squeezed to about the size of a marble, about 1 cm.

20.text:
White Dwarfs Can Explode Too

A white dwarf alone just cools. But if it has a partner star, things get interesting. A Type Ia supernova is a white dwarf that gains mass from a partner until it nears 1.4 Suns and blows apart.

Follow the steps. In a, a partner spills gas onto a white dwarf. In b, the white dwarf nears 1.4 Suns. In c, it blows apart, with no core left.

Type Ia supernovae are several times, up to about 10 times, brighter than a typical Type II, and they reach nearly the same peak every time. That makes them a standard bulb for measuring distance. In 1998, they showed the universe's expansion is speeding up, which earned the 2011 Nobel Prize for Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess.

21.text:
We Are Made of Star Stuff

Nucleosynthesis is the making of new elements by nuclear reactions in stars and star explosions. Almost every element around you was made this way.

The Big Bang made hydrogen and helium. Dying Sun-like stars make carbon and nitrogen, plus other elements through slow neutron capture (the s-process). Massive stars and supernovae make oxygen up to iron, plus some heavier elements. And neutron-star mergers make gold and strontium through fast neutron capture (the r-process).

That means the carbon in your body was made inside red giants. You are, quite literally, made of star stuff.

22.text:
Gold from Colliding Neutron Stars

On August 17, 2017, astronomers caught something new: two neutron stars merging, about 130 million light-years away. It was named GW170817. Together the two stars had about 2.7 Suns of mass.

LIGO and Virgo felt the gravitational waves, ripples in space itself, as the stars spiraled together. Gamma rays arrived 1.7 s after the merger. Then telescopes spotted a kilonova glow, powered by freshly made heavy elements, like strontium.

This was proof that neutron-star mergers forge heavy elements. Some of the gold in jewelry today may have been made in collisions like this.

26.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.1.4: compare the life cycles of stars of different masses on the H-R Diagram. Sort low, medium (like our Sun) and high mass stars by which elements they can make, and whether they can become red giants or go supernova. ES.2.3: build a model of the Sun's layers and life span. Explain how fusion in the core makes elements and energy, how that energy is carried by convection and sent out to space, including to Earth, by radiation. It also says elements heavier than iron form only in supernovae, but scientists now know more. About half of them are made by slow neutron capture (the s-process) in aging giant stars, and most of the rest by fast neutron capture (the r-process) in neutron star mergers and possibly rare supernovae.

ES.1.2 is introduced here: describe the expanding universe, or Big Bang Theory, using evidence like the Doppler effect, redshift, Hubble's Law and the cosmic microwave background. Type Ia supernovae gave you a first taste of that today.
